note: A hand-curated milestone snapshot maintained by the desk, not a live feed. Dates are announcement or first-posting dates. It exists to show one shape: physical qubit counts climbed hard through 2023, then the frontier stopped competing on raw count, and the numbers that matter moved to logical qubits, where the counts are tiny. The chart on race.html#scaling is generated from this file; tools/verify_hardware.py checks the two stay consistent.
caveats: "Qubit count" is not one number. This file separates physical from logical, but even "physical" spans fabricated sites, individually controlled qubits, and qubits good enough to compute with. IonQ's "algorithmic qubits" and various "effective" counts are a third thing again and are left out.

A logical-qubit count says nothing on its own about whether that qubit is below threshold. Only the Google 2024 entry here is a below-threshold demonstration; the others are qubits encoded and operated, not qubits that provably get better as the code grows.

Bigger has not meant better since about 2023. IBM's largest chip (Condor, 1121) predates its shift to smaller, lower-error Heron-family devices; Google's Willow (105) is smaller than its own 2019 Sycamore and is the more important machine.

milestones.note: The "quantum supremacy" chip: a sampling task in 200 seconds that Google argued would take a classical supercomputer millennia (a gap classical work later narrowed).
First IBM processor past 100 qubits; introduced the multi-level wiring that the later big chips scaled up.
Roughly a 3.4x jump in a year, and the last of IBM's chips whose headline was its size.
Neutral atoms held in optical tweezers; the first system with more than 1,000 qubit sites. Sites in a trap array, not 1,180 simultaneously computing qubits.
IBM's largest single chip, and deliberately its last of that kind: the roadmap released the same day pivots to smaller, lower-error modular processors.
Shipped alongside Condor as the actual direction: about a 3-5x lower error rate than Eagle, and the template for everything IBM has built since.
48 logical qubits from up to 280 physical atoms, with logical circuits run across them. Encoded and operated, not scaled below threshold.
Four logical qubits with a reported ~800x lower error rate than the underlying physical qubits, running thousands of operations.
24 entangled logical qubits reported on a neutral-atom machine; the largest logical-qubit count claimed to date, still not a below-threshold result.

Smaller than Sycamore. The point was not the count: it was the first processor to show a surface code getting exponentially better as the code grew (below threshold), with the logical qubit outliving its best physical qubit.
One logical qubit, at distance 7, below threshold: the first whose error rate provably falls as you add physical qubits. The number is 1 on purpose.
